common_name: Isabella Sprunt Rose (Antique Pale-Yellow Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Isabella Sprunt is an 1855 sport of the antique Tea rose Safrano, valued for its clear pale-yellow blooms and near-continuous flowering in the Gulf South's long growing season.

directions: Plant own-root stock in full sun in well-drained soil, giving it room to grow into a loose, upright shrub. Isabella Sprunt arose as a sport of the antique Tea rose Safrano in 1855, keeping its parent's elegant pointed buds and light tea fragrance but opening to a clear, soft butter-yellow rather than Safrano's apricot-orange. Like other old Tea roses it thrives on heat and humidity that frustrate modern hybrid teas, blooming in flushes almost continuously from spring through the first hard frost with minimal spray or fertilizer input. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, since old Teas bloom best on a framework of older canes rather than after hard cutting back.
sources: American Rose Society — Tea Rose Class Descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Found Rose Collections

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Avalanche is a pre-1885 multiflora tazetta that has naturalized in mild-winter Southern gardens for generations.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade in fall. Avalanche is a historic tazetta daffodil, recorded since before 1885, that carries an unusually heavy load of blooms on each stem — often a dozen or more small, fragrant white flowers with pale yellow cups clustered together, opening over a long season in late winter. Like other tazetta types it needs little winter chill and perennializes reliably in the Gulf South, multiplying steadily into large naturalized drifts when left undisturbed. Allow the foliage to yellow and die back completely before removing it so the bulbs can store enough energy for next year's heavy bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in spring or fall; in zone 9 gardens bulbs can stay in the ground year-round and be left undisturbed to bulk up into flowering clumps.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in average, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; where winters stay above the mid-20s the bulbs can remain in the ground year-round without lifting. Appleblossom is a long-grown, old-fashioned amaryllis cultivar passed hand-to-hand through Southern gardens, prized for its soft blush-pink petals brushed with white toward the center — gentler and more romantic than the bold reds of many modern hybrids. Each stout stem carries several large trumpet blooms in mid-to-late spring, appearing before or alongside the strap-shaped foliage, and established clumps flower more heavily each year if left undisturbed. Divide only when a clump becomes crowded, replanting offsets right away since the bulbs resent being stored dry out of soil for long.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Heirloom Bulbs for Texas Gardens

common_name: Honorabile Bearded Iris (Historic Bicolor Heirloom Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Honorabile is one of the oldest tall bearded iris cultivars still in commerce, introduced before 1840.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Honorabile is a pass-along bearded iris dating to before 1840 and among the oldest bicolor cultivars still commonly grown, its golden-yellow standards contrasting sharply with mahogany-red falls veined in deeper red. Shorter and tougher than most modern tall beardeds, it has survived in old homestead gardens and cemetery plantings for well over a century with no care at all, spreading steadily by rhizome offsets into dense, long-lived clumps. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor, and keep the rhizomes in full sun with excellent drainage, since standing water quickly causes rot.

common_name: Wabash Bearded Iris (Historic Dykes Medal Amoena Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Wabash won the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1940 and remains a garden-worthy heirloom bicolor.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Introduced in 1936 and awarded the American Iris Society's Dykes Medal in 1940, Wabash is a classic amoena-type bearded iris pairing crisp white standards with deep violet-purple falls, a striking two-tone combination that made it one of the most influential parents in mid-20th-century iris breeding. The sturdy stems hold their large ruffled blooms well above the fan of foliage in mid-spring, and established clumps multiply steadily, benefiting from division every three to four years to keep bloom quality high. Good drainage is essential, since soggy soil quickly leads to rhizome rot.

common_name: Amas Bearded Iris (Historic Near-Species Violet-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Amas is a historic near-species tall bearded iris collected in Turkey in the early 20th century and heavily used in early hybridizing programs.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Amas is a historic near-species bearded iris collected in Turkey in the early 1900s, its soft violet-blue flowers with a light, sweet fragrance closer in character to the wild species that gave rise to modern tall bearded hybrids. Breeders leaned on it heavily in the early 20th century for its vigor, fragrance, and reliable rebloom, and it remains a tough, easy-to-grow garden plant in its own right, spreading steadily by rhizome offsets. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom, and keep the rhizomes in full sun with sharp drainage to avoid rot.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Alcazar is a 1910 French-bred bearded iris that was hugely influential as a parent plant in early 20th-century breeding.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Introduced in France in 1910, Alcazar was one of the first tall bearded irises to combine real height and vigor with rich bicolor coloring — pale violet standards over deeper purple-blue falls — and its influence runs through the pedigree of countless later cultivars. It remains a tough, floriferous heirloom in its own right, multiplying readily into large clumps that need dividing only every three to four years to stay vigorous. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, since standing water around the rhizomes quickly leads to rot.

common_name: Madame Chereau Bearded Iris (Historic 1844 Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Madame Chereau is an 1844 French heirloom bearded iris and one of the earliest plicata (picotee-edged) cultivars still grown.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil, never burying them completely. Bred in France in 1844, Madame Chereau is among the oldest plicata-pattern bearded irises still in cultivation, its white petals finely stippled and edged in soft blue-violet along every margin, a delicate pattern that was strikingly novel for its era. Nearly two centuries in gardens have proven it a tough, dependable heirloom, multiplying steadily into long-lived clumps that ask for little beyond full sun and sharp drainage. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Silver Edge Siberian Iris (Picotee-Edged Blue-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer or early fall in moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil; Silver Edge is a 1992 Siberian iris cultivar valued for its fine picotee edging, an unusual trait in this species.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade, unlike bearded iris this species tolerates and even prefers soil that stays consistently damp. Introduced in 1992, Silver Edge is a Siberian iris prized for its fine white picotee edging around each violet-blue fall, a delicate contrast trait that is unusual in this typically solid-colored species. The narrow, grass-like foliage forms neat clumps that need no staking and hold up well through summer and fall as a textural border element long after bloom finishes in late spring. Unlike bearded iris it has no bare rhizome to rot in wet soil, making it a good choice for rain gardens or the moist edge of a pond; divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer.
